ap_psychology-m01.set_intro: A researcher recruited 50 first-year college students who all disagreed with a proposed rule that would require every student to attend a 7:00 A.M. exercise class. Using random assignment, she placed 25 students in each of two conditions. Each student recorded an audio message urging classmates to support the rule. Students in the first condition were paid $2 for the recording, and students in the second condition were paid $40. Afterward, an assistant who did not know which payment each student had received asked the student to rate his or her own agreement with the rule from 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree). The table shows the results.

stimulus.description: Agreement with the rule by payment condition

items.stem: Which concept best explains why the students paid $2 reported more agreement with the rule than the students paid $40?

options.text: Cognitive dissonance reduction
options.why: Students paid very little had weak outside justification for arguing against their own view, so they may have shifted their attitude to reduce the tension between their behavior and their belief.

options.text: The central route to persuasion
options.why: The central route changes attitudes through careful evaluation of argument quality, but the payment amount says nothing about argument quality.

options.text: The foot-in-the-door phenomenon
options.why: That phenomenon involves agreeing to a small request first, which raises later compliance with a larger request, and no larger request was made here.

options.text: The fundamental attribution error
options.why: That error is overemphasizing personality and underemphasizing situations when explaining other people's behavior, which is not what the ratings measure.

items.stem: Why was the assistant who collected the agreement ratings not told which payment each student had received?

options.text: To ensure that students understood the true purpose of the study before rating
options.why: Explaining the purpose to students is the job of a debriefing, and keeping the assistant uninformed does not provide one.

options.text: To help the results apply to students at other colleges
options.why: Generalizability depends on how the sample was selected from the population, not on what the assistant knew.

options.text: To guarantee that the two payment groups were equal in size
options.why: Group size was set by randomly assigning 25 students to each condition, not by keeping the assistant uninformed.

options.text: To keep expectations from influencing how ratings were taken
options.why: Keeping the data collector unaware of the condition helps prevent his or her expectations from shaping how responses are gathered or recorded.

options.text: On average, students paid $2 reported more agreement with the rule than students paid $40.

options.text: The ratings varied so differently between the conditions that the means cannot be compared.

options.why: The mean of 3.2 in the $40 condition is below the scale midpoint of 5, which reflects disagreement.

ap_psychology-m02.set_intro: A 24-year-old graduate student sought help because she could not leave her apartment without checking the stove and the door lock over and over. She knew the checks were unnecessary, but skipping them made her intensely anxious, and the routine made her late to class most mornings. A clinician asked her to record the total minutes she spent checking on a typical day and then worked with her in weekly sessions. The table shows her self-recorded daily checking time at three points.

items.stem: Which disorder best fits the student's symptoms?

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
options.why: Repeated checking performed to relieve intense anxiety, even though the person recognizes it as unnecessary, is characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder.

options.text: Panic disorder
options.why: That disorder involves sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms, not a daily routine of checking.

options.text: Major depressive disorder
options.why: That disorder centers on persistent low mood or loss of interest, which the description does not mention.

options.text: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.why: That disorder involves persistent, hard-to-control worry about many topics rather than a repeated ritual performed to relieve anxiety.

items.stem: In one session, the clinician had her stand near the stove, deliberately not check it, and stay with her anxiety until it faded. This approach is best described as

options.text: Free association to uncover unconscious conflicts
options.why: Free association is a psychodynamic technique for exploring unconscious material and does not involve confronting a feared situation.

options.text: Exposure with response prevention
options.why: Facing a feared situation while resisting the usual ritual is a behavioral treatment that lets the anxiety decline without the checking.

options.text: Person-centered therapy with unconditional positive regard
options.why: Person-centered therapy relies on an accepting listener rather than on deliberately facing a feared situation.

options.text: Electroconvulsive therapy for severe symptoms
options.why: Electroconvulsive therapy is a biomedical treatment, and the clinician used no medical procedure in this session.

items.stem: Which statement is best supported by the table?

options.text: Her checking time declined across the weeks, but one person's record cannot show why.
options.why: Each recorded value is lower than the one before it, and a single self-reported case cannot establish what caused the decline.

options.text: Her recorded checking time dropped by more than half between the start of treatment and week 4.
options.why: A drop from 180 to 95 minutes is a decrease of 85 minutes, which is less than half of 180.

options.text: Her recorded checking time rose briefly after treatment began and then fell again by week 8.
options.why: The table shows no rise; each recorded value is lower than the value before it.

options.text: These results demonstrate that the treatment reduces checking for most people with the disorder.
options.why: A single self-reported case cannot show how a treatment works for most people with a disorder.
